title: Cosmic bubble NGC 6781
caption: The planetary nebula NGC 6781, imaged by the ESO 3.6-metre telescope

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: Shells of gas glow in intricate patterns around a faint central star in this picture of NGC 6781, a planetary nebula in the direction of the constellation Aquila, the Eagle.

Stars like our Sun lack the mass to end their lives as supernovae. Instead, before fading into dense, Earth-sized embers called white dwarfs, they cast off colourful shells of gas. These are known as planetary nebulae, a misleading name that comes from how these round clouds resembled giant planets through small telescopes.

Inside NGC 6781, shells of gas blown off the surface of the faint but very hot central star are expanding into space. Harsh ultraviolet light from the star makes them shine. Over time the star will steadily cool and darken until it disappears from view.
scale: The nebula lies a few thousand light-years away and is approximately two light-years across, according to ESO.

understand.summary: The EFOSC2 instrument on the ESO 3.6-metre telescope took this visible-light image through B, V and R filters plus hydrogen-alpha and oxygen filters; the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Narrow-band filters and long exposures reveal glowing shells too faint and too finely coloured for the eye.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The image was captured with EFOSC2, the ESO Faint Object Spectrograph and Camera, on the 3.6-metre telescope at La Silla Observatory in Chile. It used three wide-band filters and two narrow-band ones, and EFOSC2's field of view is 4.1 by 4.1 arcminutes.
alt: Glowing shells of gas in intricate patterns around a faint central star.
